about: The first prayer of the Canon. In medieval missals the T of “Te” was drawn as a cross, and out of that letter grew the full-page Crucifixion that stands before the Canon in the old missal. The prayer names what lies on the altar three times over — dona, múnera, sacrifícia — and the priest signs the cross at each of the three. It also names the Church, the Pope and the local bishop; the word orthodóxus occurs nowhere else in the whole Ordinary of the Mass.

s01.narrative: After the Sanctus the priest raises his eyes and hands, lowers them at once and bows low over the altar, laying his hands upon it. From here to the end of the Canon he speaks silently.

s02.translation: Thee therefore, most merciful Father, through Iesus Christ thy Son our Lord, we humbly pray and beseech,

s03.narrative: The priest kisses the altar and joins his hands before his breast.

s04.translation: that thou hold as accepted and bless

s05.narrative: Three signs of the cross together over the host and the chalice.

s06.translation: these gifts, these offerings, these holy and unblemished sacrifices,

s07.narrative: The priest spreads his hands and goes on.

s08.translation: which we offer thee first of all for thy holy catholic Church: deign to keep her in peace, to guard, to unite and to govern her throughout the whole world:

s09.translation: together with thy servant our Pope, and our Bishop, and all the orthodox, who keep the catholic and apostolic faith.

w001.function: The object stands first, twelve words before the verbs “rogámus” (w013) and “pétimus” (w015) — the Canon opens with the one addressed.

w002.function: The therefore reaches back to the Sanctus: since heaven and earth are full of thy glory, therefore we ask thee.

w003.function: A superlative in the vocative; the same word turns up further on as a name — Cleméntis in the Communicántes.

w004.function: The Canon addresses the Father, not Christ: the whole offering goes through the Son to the Father.

w008.function: In apposition to “Christum” (w007), and so accusative.

w012.function: An adjective, not an adverb: it agrees with the unstated “we” and says in what posture we ask — bent low.

w016.function: An older form of ut; not the infinitive of utor (to use), though it is spelt the same.

w017.function: Accépta habére is a phrase from accounting: to enter something as received. The adjective agrees with three nouns that do not arrive until after the rubric.

w021.function: Three times “these”, and a sign of the cross at each: the prayer is pointing at what lies on the corporal.

w024.function: A munus is a gift that is owed — a due, a duty; a donum is freely given.

w028.function: From libáre, to take a portion from an offering; illibáta is an offering nothing has been taken from.

w030.function: In primis has set as a whole and no longer marks a gender — which is why none is given here.

w031.function: An accusative neuter plural relative: it reaches back to gifts, offerings and sacrifices at once.

w039.function: Feminine, because Ecclésia is feminine in Latin; the four infinitives that follow all take it as their object.

w040.function: One verb for what English needs several words to say: to grant peace to someone.

w045.function: The four infinitives all hang on this one verb, which comes only after them.

w046.function: An ablative of place with no preposition — Latin does without in here.

w048.function: Orbis terrárum, the circle of the lands, is the Roman name for the whole known world.

w049.function: The ablative of unus set hard as an adverb: una cum means together with.

w054.function: Here the missal prints N., and the priest names the reigning Pope. This edition does not print the blank, because it is not a Latin word.

w056.function: Antístes — literally one who stands before; in pagan Latin the priest of a temple.

w057.function: The missal's second N.: the name of the local bishop. The priest names his own ordinary, not the bishop of whatever diocese he happens to be in.

w060.function: From Greek orthós, straight, and dóxa, opinion. Not the name of a communion but a description of those who hold the Church's faith.

w062.function: A genitive agreeing with “fídei” (w065); the adjectives run two words ahead of their noun.

w066.function: From cólere, which means both to till and to worship; cultóres fídei are those who cultivate the faith as a field.
